commentBody:
Nearly half my Saturday average time.

Smooth sailing!

That was a fun puzzle to solve!

But it was far from qualified to be a NYT Saturday puzzle. There were just way too many clues that were immediately guessable with no crossings.

When I went to IRAN, I picked up two things at the airport duty free to take home. A big bag of pistachios for my dad. And a tin of caviar for myself.

Shortly after I bought it, I realized that there was no way it would keep for 24 hours until I get back home. So I got a plastic spoon from an airport vendor and went to the smoking lounge. Ate it straight out of the tin while I smoked a Cuban. Honestly a top ten travel moment of my life

And after a challenging Friday the Great Easening resumes. This was the fastest Saturday in a long time.  Almost no friction.

Reality checking, XWStats currently shows "Average".

Sigh.  What can we do...  :(

It looks like I'm not the only one who found this puzzle enjoyable, but not Saturday-difficult. This was my fastest Saturday solve ever, barely longer than 1/3 my average Saturday time. Based on solve time, this was between Tuesday and Wednesday.

I’m sorry for the constructor’s loss. 

The puzzle was nice. I think easier than yesterday? But an engaging solve.  

I was sure I was gonna have to fly speck EREADER. but was surprised when the gold showed up immediately after the last cell. 
I dutifully went to Google to figure out what this word meant. Only then did I realize. That I was e-tricked. 

I’ve never heard of banana cake. Bread yes. And the only upside down I’ve ever heard of is pineapple upside down cake.  I thought it was gonna be Bundt cake. Just my experience. 

“I’m outraged” if one of my favorite sarcastic expressions. If I’m actually outraged. I use a word that starts with P. and can mean drunk in some parts of the world. 

YES NO DOUBT. sounds weird to me. Yes followed by no.  Like that coat is a little big. 

Anyway. Fun puzzle.

Quadruple stacks, you don’t see that every day.  I especially like I’M OUTRAGED followed by DON’T STRESS.

I love the ROAD WIN clue [Success in another’s field, say]. Very clever. 

Well done, Adrian.
A nice challenge. Started slow but once they started falling I picked up speed. Had a little trouble with the NE corner because of the questionable YESNODOUBT.
Fairly breezy this time. Nice!

How many versions of, “I finished this fast, it wasn’t a worthy __day puzzle” must we read?

Get over yourself! Try limiting your comments to what you appreciate about the puzzle. I guarantee you’ll be a happier person when you start seeing the good rather than focusing on your dissatisfaction.
this was a learner for me. lots of learning to be had, not a super satisfying solve. we all have those, though. good puzzle.
I admit I searched for Adam. He sounds like a very nice, talented person who is gone too soon. I'm sorry for your loss.
PB for me. More of a Tuesday than a Saturday. I’m not complaining. I rather enjoyed it. It was nice easy solve after yesterday.
I was having a hard time putting what might end up in my mattress out of my head, wondering if I should check on it later.

"Did you get to the part yet where the driver installs those aerodynamic devices--"
"Hey! No spoilers!"

(From "The Sunroof Also Rises")

Okay, I'm going to admit that I shook myself up a martini and moved out on the garden balcony and prepared myself for a nice long, enjoyable, head scratcher. Instead, I finished it in less than a third of my martini, and that includes taking sips of martini obviously. 

That said, I do think it was an enjoyable puzzle. There was some fun pairrs and the what might wind up in your mattress clue was very humorously provocative. Was that KEPTITPG? Har! 😏

I really enjoyed entering QAT, one of my favorite lifesaving Scrabble entries. I didn't look it up but I don't remember seeing it in any of the crossword puzzles I've done over the last few years.  

Really like the clue for ROADWIN too. 

Really a nice one, I liked it, but I do have to admit that while IMnotOUTRAGED, the only thing I didn't plug in pretty quickly and correctly was the let me think about it clue...  Was it hmm, erm, oh...  it's UHH. 

My condolences to our fine constructor, Mr Johnson, on your great loss. What a lovely tribute to what sounds like an amazing human!  May his memory continue to bless your life for all of your days.

There was lots of fun in this one.  Only in a crossword can one find a menu with German RABBITSTEW, Greek FETACHEESE, and American BANANACAKE.  I also liked that the puzzle ended in the SE corner with IMOUTRAGED followed by DONTSTRESS.
Nice Saturday. A couple of educated guesses made it a relatively simple solve, but enjoyable nevertheless.
All I could see was YESNOproBs despite all the evidence to the contrary ie KEEPITPG wouldn’t suddenly become KEEPIsPG 🤣

Nothing too stretchy about this puzzle—I agree it was on the easier side—but it was very fun and elegantly constructed. Those 4 stacks on both corners were beautiful. I also enjoyed the clues for ROADWIN, EREADER and FETACHEESE and that funny entry KEEPITPG (I admit I had KEEPITPC at first).

I really thought I would be the first to bring up Laverne and Shirley, great call out Caitlin.

Also happy to see a tribute to TERIGARR—we see her a lot in these puzzles but not her full name. I would add a role in a really offbeat comedy “After Hours” and of course I never leave out a Star Trek reference, she had a very fun role jn “Assignment: Earth”.

Anyone else have MINT before SHIP in the Icebreaker clue? (of course, then it would have been two words).

Adrian, what a great tribute to a great musician and I enjoyed listening to the clip, thank you for sharing.
Tasty with some crunchy toppings. Unlike the road kill rabbit stew I once ate while ski instructing in New Zealand. And yes, I found a hare in it.

I also thought this was pretty easy for a Saturday, but I'll be honest: I'll personally take a well-constructed easy puzzle over one that's artificially (imo) challenging because it includes a bunch of naticks and proper name trivia any day. 

(Of course a good challenging puzzle with tricky cluing that minimizes naticks is the best, but I've found that pretty rare in my years of playing.)

I loved Teri Garr. An underrated actress who could be funny and heartbreaking at the same time. Tootsie may be a little dated now, but it was a great movie and people should seek it out. She was also terrific in Young Frankenstein and After Hours. But my favorite Teri Garr role may have been that of the quirky, flirty recurring guest on the David Letterman Show who was always up for a gag, no matter how weird or potentially embarrassing. Such a unique talent.

What the --- I thought for sure we'd be hearing from a host of vegan zealots about the hasenpfeffer lead-off. In fact, the puzzle is a dialog on this:
Vegan Zealot: "I'm outraged!"
Mr. Emu: "Don't stress, it's just a puzzle, dude, not a call to kill rabbits."
VZ: "Knock knock, anyone home at the Times? I'm in extremis here!"
ME: "Don't be gross. Keep it PG. Put your bifocals on and focus your eyes on the rarely seen white tiger. Chew some qat...yes, no doubt you'll---"
VZ: "Feta cheese, BBQs, slaw on fish tacos, where will it end? But you greet my argument with snark and kid around with me. I don't give a shag when you call me a banana cake! So what if I am?"
ME: "The Emu Brethren have met and have concluded that what anyone has eaten is of no-one else's concern, and that since we tolerate no spoilers, you are hereby deported to Columbia (your choice which one). Teri Garr will drive you there in her mini-car, and yes there is no doubt that soon you'll go the op-ed route..."

After yesterday's defeat, that was lovely. Thank you!

Took a shot in the dark for rabbit stew, and the rest of the puzzle gave way like braised meat.

I seem to be in the minority in finding today's puzzle much tougher than yesterday's. What a fun challenge! I really loved the clever cluing. "Success in another's field" gave me such a great aha moment when I figured it out.
Seemed like a Friday puzzle to me...

Thanks to this puzzle for teaching me the fact about box jellyfish, who not only have 24 true eyes but can apparently learn without a centralized brain! (I was disappointed that the "success in another's field" clue had nothing to do with poaching, though.)
Thank you so much for the tidbits of Greek culture. I enjoyed them immensely. They were neither tragic nor epic.
I’m sorry for your loss Andrian.

7D [Author Silverstein] SHEL wrote and illustrated a really nice book, "The Giving Tree," great for children or adults, I think. Here is actor Keith Carradine reading it: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BgKVBhO6GkU Did you also know that there is a USPS stamp in his honor? https://about.usps.com/newsroom/national-releases/2022/0408-usps-giving-tree-forever-stamp.htm

Ah I loved this! A real tough, gnarly Saturday I had to struggle through, always thinking I’d never get there, but in the end did. 
I had NEAT for REAL for so long and KEEPITPC and not PG too…. Felt so good in the end…

Fri and Sat normally crush me. I had my best ever combined time for the two days 18+22.  

What was that old candy ad, "Sometimes you feel like a nut, sometimes you don't."
EREADER absolutely bammed my boozle for a long time. I was pretty sure of all the crossing words, but just couldn't parse it.

I’m cross about KEEP IT PG. It should obviously be PC. That one clue took me ages and in the end i had to cheat by reading the wordplay column. I actually started off wondering if “Refrain from foul language, say” could solve to “forswear”. 

Overall i quite liked the puzzle, but ROADWIN was new to me and not terribly convincing. 

And i got stuck with bad eyesight - i thought “Fellow fellows” said “Fellow felons” so i struggled trying to fit “cellmates” into eight letters. I guess i need BIFOCALS.

Caught the crossword puzzle solving bug so long ago, the T.V. Guide cost a whopping 15 cents. And on this late, summery Saturday, I, at long last completed a NYT’s Saturday sans any form of mystical (or any other form) prompting. ‘Tis been a journey. Thanks Adrian J. et al for the puzz; it resulted in my beating some fairly steep ODDS. 😀

BYE(S) Youse Guys,

Bru

Luckily there are no box jellies around here, but I did see a lions mane yesterday while body surfing,  Due to the warming water, they're becoming a lot more common.  Boo!  

I thought this puzzle had some pretty clever clues.  [Tied up with] for DREW and [Volume control device] for EREADER had me scratching my head.  More like that would be a good thing.
@Becky A good start the season

somehow this puzzle just clicked for me and i raced through it. Felt like a Wednesday, almost.  Nice to see Desi Lydic get a shout out. I remember her on the Daily Show way back when when she was pregnant but still clever and funny and smart. Onward!
Here in the Boston suburbs we're overrun with wild rabbits eating everyone's flowers, so RABBITSTEW should definitely be on more people's menus.

Terrific grid design – a NYT debut design, by the way – that allowed for those two four-stacks and ten ten-letter answers, all colorful.  When you pack the box with loveliness like that, you give the solver beauty and enrichment on top of riddle-ment, deepening the joy.

Certainly for me.  This was a gift.  

My favorite answer: KEEP IT PG.  My favorite clue: A tie between [Success in another’s field, say] for ROAD WIN, and [Volume control device?] for E-READER.

I love the German “pf”, as in pfeffer or kopf.  It’s pfun to say.  

And what a terrific RABBIThole I went through upon seeing UPSTART, when I realized you could reverse it to “startup”.  Words like that, I learned, are called reverse compound words. They are legion in our language, i.e., breakout, boathouse, oversleep, lookout, holdup, takeover, and trackside.

Bounty in the box today.  Thank you, Adrian.  I loved this!
Everything I know about hasenpfeffer I learned from Yosemite Sam.

Much, much too easy for a Saturday puzzle. Only the NE offered any resistance at all. 

Nice enough, but another "themeless Wednesday" given the far too direct cluing of so many entries.

Done in about a quarter of yesterday's time ... and now I feel obligated to turn to my work. Sigh.
Before I even start today's puzzle, I just wanted to say that I wish the Midi would have accepted Roman numerals for the pool balls. That's it. That's the whole comment.
Oh, this was highly delicious, starting with 1A and getting tastier. Well done, Adrian! Read the c-notes :(
Regarding the spelling bee: do the editors find the word nutria offensive?  It is a valid and relatively common word and I can't think of a reason it is not accepted.
I don’t get banana cake clue. Made upside down?
I got 6D easy enough, which meant 35A _MUST_ be RADIO, right?! It held me up until it was the last word, and only by peeking. KEEPITPG made me panic when all I had TPG

Ok, it’s after, so let’s talk about it.
[“Into each life some ____ must fall”: Longfellow]

Now that clue is a spoiler, if I ever saw one.
Hail?
Leaves?
Snow?
Anvils?
Volcanic ash?
Dew?
Arches?
Another blue star Saturday, but a nice challenge. I think 40D should be "on" another field, not "in". No one plays "in" the field.

This was fun. About a third of my Saturday average, and less than a minute off my best. 

A friend of mine makes pineapple upside down cake every week; maybe if I had ever heard of BANANA upside down CAKE I would have had a PB.

Got BIFOCALS right away. I wasn't so sure about WESSON as a competitor for Crisco: I only think of Crisco in terms of the solid shortening I used to use for pie crust (butter all the way now) and WESSON only for oil, but I assume there must be some overlap.

Living in the smallest state capital, where our high school teams are called the Solons, I was hoping for that until I counted the squares in SOLDON.

Thanks!
The Midi:   I love it - a rebus series in the Midi.   Some people will squawk.

I was expecting something tricky for 1 Across, but not to be. And so it went. It's always bittersweet to see TERI GARR in the puzzle these days, so in her honor I'll just post her big scene from Tootsie. https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=HrmWPBvzpqo
Great grid - I enjoyed the stacks and “mini-stacks” in the NE and SW.
Whoosh!

We particularly liked "Success in another's field, say"/ROADWIN.

It is a wonderful thing to have these puzzles to enjoy every day.
Haven't read the comments yet, but I feel it's safe to assume somebody has already linked to Hare-N-Pepa's smash hit "Whatta Jack".
“Maybe you can help me straighten out my Longfellow”
Friday and Saturday puzzles this week were almost identical as far as difficulty goes.  Easier than I expected once I got a few fills.
On the EREADER I just don’t get the control part. Volume device would have been better

I always find I’m on the same page as Adrian Johnson. 

If I have a hunch or an impulse about the response to one of his clues, more often than not my instinct is right. That doesn’t happen with other constructors. 

In his Constructor Note, he mentions wanting to be great in this industry. 

In books, Adrian, you are!

When I see your bye line, I know I’m in for a fun solve. 

Thank you!
I agree with the comments but did not enjoy the disconnects. Sheesh!!

I hadn't heard of ROAD WIN but someone has kindly explained. 

BRETHERN is one of the few words that take the old plural of -en, like oxen and children. 

Is SNARK related to the Lewis Carroll poem? I would say snide or sarky (sarcastic). I don't use snit either - it's strop. And a person is more likely to be called snotty rather than a snot.

An analogy regarding the Great Easening just came to me while responding in another thread, and I like it enough to double-post it…

Imagine all the folks who complain about the puzzles being too easy are avid bowlers, most of whom have been competing in a league for years/decades, and one day we come into the only bowling alley within 100 miles to find that management has installed permanent bumpers on all the lanes.

Naturally, we’re all pretty bummed; but a bunch of beginners are out on the lanes having a good time, and they tell us we should stop complaining and either learn to enjoy bowling with bumpers or find a new hobby.

To anyone who thinks this analogy is an exaggeration: please go solve the Saturday puzzles from August 2007 (a month I happened to recently visit in the archives), and let me know how that goes.

Well, not all that easy for me, of course, and I did have to look up a couple of things. But ended up being an enjoyable workout. And... puzzle find today - A Sunday from October 12, 2008 by Rich Norris with the title: "Change of Heart." Some theme answers, all cleverly clued: DUTCHSTEWINDIES LONEARTSSTATE SHAGGYGODSTORY GENERALPOTSOFFICE INCOOLPARENTIS THREELIMEISLAND Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=10/12/2008&h=42a I'm done. ....

Happy Saturday! My stars! If such an interesting puzzle can’t have an interesting poem then I don’t know what the world’s coming to:

a/ let’s talk about hasenpfeffer
straight up, tonight! wind up the windows and haul this jellyfish in — scratch this mattres from shrub to leaves from impossible to carolina to upside down… show this dish what what is and what is what d/ and stevie nicks and hacky sack but absolutely each variety of arriviste hairstyle while you and i beat the wine list and engage the a/ elements in rabbit stew
As a retired engineer, I was happily surprised to see BOXPLOT. It took me back to the days of combing through data, looking for good and bad experimental outcomes. Probably done by A.L. now.

Umm....UHH...who makes BANANACAKE upside down? I make a very rich banana layer cake with very dark chocolate frosting for my own birthday every year. My Nana quit baking when I was 8, and someone had to take over! (But...I always like a good banana recipe!)
Got off to a bad start, I was sure that "Benjamin Franklin invention of the 1780s" was CATLASER.
Yes, no doubt: Thinking of Elmer Fudd thinking of rabbit stew. Darn wabbit! No spoilers but he never gets to taste it. I had "Keep it IN" instead of PG for awhile until picturing the shag haircuts.
Not tough yet still satisfying. Not ridiculously easy.

Ah,  COLUMBIA, SC, --where my great-great-grandfather practiced medicine and married a Sims--was the birthplace of his son of the same name--who wed a Boulware; HE was seen to have "married up" until things went so badly for the Army of the Confederacy (in which he had invested heavily...oops)   Too bad the forebears hadn't stayed in Scotland!  

BOX PLOT?  Box jellyfish?  SHAC?  ROAD WIN?
Dipped (out) for SNUCK?
A *DRAW* is a TIE, but "Tied up with" = DREW???

Just a touch too far.  As with my South Carolina forebears, I thiink the bloodlines got too drawn out...diluted, as it were.  Well, it's hard to know why some of our BRETHREN didn't amount to much, but it seems to have been convenient to blame it on ELEMENTS such as the bloodlines.... (or the lack of reliable birth control.)

A worthy Saturday.  While I'm salivating, literally and figuratively, to talk to you about hasenpfeffer, I guess I'd better begin with the rest of the puzzle:

I think ROAD WIN (40D) is a world-class clue.  Fooled me completely before it filled in.  I was wondering if I would ever score a success in, say, rocket science.

The NE was impossible until I thought to change NEAT for "straight-up" to REAL.  And I finally figured out why E READER is a "volume control device."  Another world-class clue.

Now onto my beloved hasenpfeffer -- which is NOT a RABBIT STEW.  It's a hare stew.  I was pretty sure that a rabbit is not a hare, but I looked it up just to be sure.  And it's not!

If you have had RABBIT STEW, it can be a lovely and delicate dish with a lot of flavor.  Or, in less talented hands, it can be pretty flavorless and forgettable.  But hasenpfeffer is rich, rich, rich, made with a rich brown sauce -- very gamy and absolutely scrumptious.

There was a German restaurant from my youth on East 86th Street called Jager House.  They had two really unique and memorable dishes:  Hasenpfeffer and Saddle of Hare with Preiselberries (sp?)  Both incredible.  Their 3-course dinner cost -- wait for it! -- $4.95!!!!  And no, the first course wasn't tomato juice or fruit cup -- I always had the Shrimp Cocktail.  Their sinful dessert choices were to die for.

They don't make restaurants like that anymore -- and certainly not at those 1950-ish prices.

Today certainly a contender for "Constructor Comments of the Year".  Fun puzzle with clever clues.  Also finished up yesterday's, which was tough with all the unknown names.  Stull stuck on Thursday though - I refuse to peek at the answers.

Ben Franklin is “commonly credited” with the invention of the item, but historians are skeptical. There is no definitive source proving he did, and there are other claimants to their invention.

Shame that you have a historical myth presented as fact in a clue.

Never have I ever--
--heard of "Banana Upside-down Cake."
At least not intentionally. Accidents happen, pans slip from your oven mitts onto the floor.
Pineapples, yes--but consider other acidic fruits: apricots, or even GAGE plums. And of course, there's always Tarte des Demoiselles Tatins . . . .
But bananas? Not acidic enough, and will break down and become watery during baking. I'm not saying one CAN'T make Banana upside-down cake--but not "commonly."

After a very quick Friday, my prediction of a Saturday slog was demolished by a new Saturday PB. I am not getting that much better at this. Sorry for all the excellent solvers who must be very frustrated at the change in the weekend puzzles. This was a nice puzzle, and a poignant constructor's note. Thanks Adrian and sorry for your loss.

"All that a man has to say or do that can possibly concern mankind, is in some shape or other to tell the story of his love (...) – Henry David Thoreau Adrian, you always tell the story of your love of construction in each and every puzzle you create for us. More than that, you always tell the story of your love for others in your constructor notes, be they family, friends, acquaintances, co-constructors, mentors or editors. Every note you write is a glimpse into the mensch you are and the value that you place on the existence of those other than your own self. Thank you for sharing with us the love letter to your friend. I am very sorry that the opportunity to make new memories has been taken from you. But please be at peace trusting that every dear one that departs stays alive in our treasure trove of the memories we already have, and the story of our love goes on. (Reposting your friend's beautiful piano rendition of Lord Huron's "The Night We Met" for those who missed it in your notes- https://youtu.be/ZYCRdRRNOuI?si=HzL0NnmLzheBT5178)

Thanks to the team for a terrific puzzle.

I have been doing the NYT puzzles most days since 2023. It took me about a year to consistently solve without lookups, and that was such a fun year!! It felt amazing to develop the skill.

Until fairly recently, I found Friday and Saturday puzzles to be quite challenging and every once in a while, I couldn't finish one. 

Yesterday felt like that! I did finish, but it was slow and very satisfying. Today I solved in 1/4 of yesterday's time, and it was still fun, but also much less difficult than yesterday; hence, less satisfying. 

It makes me a little sad to see this happening. I very much want puzzles to be accessible to new solvers, but IMO, having the average difficulty factor be so much lower than even a few years ago takes away the true joy of learning to get good at puzzles! 

I'd love to see Fridays and Saturdays return to their prior difficulty levels. I think having 7 days of puzzles allows for this!!! ...and I've read enough comments from constructors on these pages to know that they would like to keep creating hard puzzles and publishing them in the NYT. 

Just my $0.02. ❤️🥳
